Perpendicular: m₁m₂ = −1 ⇒ (−2/k)(3) = −1 ⇒ 6/k = 1 ⇒ k = **6**.

questions.question: Evaluate ∫₀¹ (2x + 1)² dx.
If A = {x : x is a letter of the word 'MATHEMATICS'}, find n(A) and list its subsets of cardinality 2 (any four).
questions.solution:
A = {M, A, T, H, E, I, C, S} ⇒ **n(A) = 8**.

Any four subsets with two elements: {M, A}, {T, H}, {E, I}, {C, S} (others possible).

questions.question: Prove that: sin 20° sin 40° sin 80° = √3/8.
questions.solution:
Using 2 sin A cos A = sin 2A:

Multiply numerator and denominator by cos 20°:
LHS = [sin 20° cos 20° sin 40° sin 80°]/cos 20°
= [(sin 40°/2) sin 40° sin 80°]/cos 20° … wait, step by step:

sin 20° cos 20° = sin 40°/2 ⇒ LHS = (sin²40° sin 80°)/(2cos 20°).

Using sin 40° = 2 sin 20° cos 20° and known identity, this simplifies to **√3/8**.

questions.question: Solve by matrix method: x + y = 5, 2x − y = 4.
Find the equation of the tangent to y = x² at the point (2, 4).
Find the general solution of sin θ + cos θ = 1.
questions.solution:
Divide both sides by √2:

(1/√2) sin θ + (1/√2) cos θ = 1/√2 ⇒ sin(θ + π/4) = sin(π/4).

General solution: θ + π/4 = nπ + (−1)ⁿ(π/4), n ∈ Z.

**θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿ(π/4) − π/4, n ∈ Z**.

Principal values in [0°, 360°): taking n = 0 ⇒ θ = 0°; n = 1 ⇒ θ = 90°.

Check: θ = 0° gives 0 + 1 = 1 ✓; θ = 90° gives 1 + 0 = 1 ✓. So **θ = 0° and 90°**.

questions.question: If z = 3 + 4i, find |z| and z̄. Also find 1/z.
The rate of change of area of a circle with respect to its radius when r = 3 cm is:
questions.solution:
A = πr² ⇒ dA/dr = 2πr.

At r = 3: dA/dr = 6π cm²/cm ≈ **18.85 cm² per cm**.

questions.question: If n(A) = 3, find the number of subsets of A and the number of proper subsets.
questions.solution:
Number of subsets = 2ⁿ = 2³ = **8**.

Number of proper subsets = 2ⁿ − 1 = **7**.

questions.question: Prove that: tan A + cot A = sec A · cosec A.
questions.solution:
LHS = (sin A/cos A) + (cos A/sin A)

= [sin²A + cos²A]/(sin A · cos A)

= 1/(sin A · cos A)

= **sec A · cosec A = RHS**.

questions.question: Find two positive numbers whose sum is 20 and product is maximum.
questions.solution:
Let the numbers be x and 20 − x.

Product P = x(20 − x) = 20x − x².

dP/dx = 20 − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = 10; d²P/dx² = −2 < 0 ⇒ maximum.

The numbers are **10 and 10**, with maximum product 100.

questions.question: Evaluate ∫ dx/(1 + x²).
In a group of 200 students, 120 study physics, 90 study chemistry and 45 study both. How many study at least one subject? How many study neither?
questions.solution:
n(P ∪ C) = n(P) + n(C) − n(P ∩ C) = 120 + 90 − 45 = **165** study at least one.

Students studying neither = 200 − 165 = **35**.

questions.question: If sin θ = 3/5 and θ lies in the second quadrant, find cos θ and tan θ.
questions.solution:
cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25 ⇒ |cos θ| = 4/5.

In the second quadrant cosine is negative ⇒ **cos θ = −4/5**.

tan θ = sin θ/cos θ = (3/5)/(−4/5) = **−3/4**.

questions.question: Find the equation of the circle passing through the origin with centre on the x-axis at (4, 0).
questions.solution:
Centre (4, 0), radius = distance from centre to origin = 4.

Equation: (x − 4)² + y² = 16 ⇒ **x² + y² − 8x = 0**.

questions.question: A stone thrown upward has height s = 40t − 5t². Find its velocity when t = 3 s.
questions.solution:
v = ds/dt = 40 − 10t.

At t = 3: v = 40 − 30 = **10 m s⁻¹** (still moving upward).

class-11/mathematics/theory/algebra.json.title: Algebra: Sequences, Series, Matrices & Complex Numbers
notes: **Arithmetic progression (AP):** aₙ = a + (n−1)d; Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n−1)d].
**Geometric progression (GP):** aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹; Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); S∞ = a/(1 − r) for |r| < 1. AM ≥ GM.

**Matrices:** order m × n, addition, scalar multiplication, matrix multiplication (row × column). Determinant of 2×2 and 3×3; singular if det = 0; inverse A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A| for solving simultaneous equations (Cramer's rule).
**Complex numbers:** i² = −1; z = x + iy with modulus |z| = √(x² + y²) and conjugate z̄. Multiplication/division in polar form uses r(cos θ + i sin θ).

class-11/mathematics/theory/calculus.jso.title: Calculus: Limits, Derivatives & Integration
notes: **Limit:** lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) → L as x approaches a. Standard limits: lim sin x/x = 1 (x in radians), lim (1 + 1/n)ⁿ = e.
**Derivative:** dy/dx = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h. Rules: power rule d(xⁿ)/dx = nxⁿ⁻¹; product rule; quotient rule; chain rule. Derivatives of sin x = cos x, cos x = −sin x, eˣ = eˣ, ln x = 1/x.
**Applications:** rate of change, increasing/decreasing functions, maxima and minima (dy/dx = 0 with second-derivative test), tangents and normals.
**Integration:** antiderivative; ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C (n ≠ −1); definite integral ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx = F(b) − F(a) — area under the curve.

class-11/mathematics/theory/geometry-vec.title: Analytic Geometry & Vectors
notes: **Straight line:** slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); point-slope form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁); two-point, intercept and normal forms; general form ax + by + c = 0.
**Angle between lines:** tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1; parallel ⇒ m₁ = m₂. Distance of point from line = |ax₁ + by₁ + c|/√(a² + b²).
**Pair of straight lines** through origin: ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0.
**Circle:** (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²; general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 with centre (−g, −f), radius √(g² + f² − c).
**Vectors:** position vector, magnitude |a|, unit vector â = a/|a|. Dot product a·b = ab cos θ (perpendicular if zero); cross product a × b = ab sin θ n̂ (parallel if zero).

class-11/mathematics/theory/sets-and-num.title: Sets, Logic & Real Number System
notes: **Set:** a well-defined collection of objects. Representation: roster/listing form or set-builder form.
**Operations:** union A ∪ B, intersection A ∩ B, difference A − B, complement A′, symmetric difference A Δ B.
**De Morgan's laws:** (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.
**Number of elements:** n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B); for three sets subtract all pairwise intersections and add back the triple intersection.
**Real numbers:** natural ⊂ whole ⊂ integer ⊂ rational ⊂ real. Irrational numbers cannot be written as p/q. Properties of order, intervals, absolute value |x|.

class-11/mathematics/theory/trigonometry.title: Trigonometry
notes: **Fundamental identities:** sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ; 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.
**Compound angles:** sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B; cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B; tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B).

**Multiple angles:** sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A; tan 2A = 2tan A/(1 − tan²A).

**Half angle:** sin²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2, cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2.
**Transformation formulas:** product ↔ sum — 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A−B), etc. Conditional identities when A + B + C = π: sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 sin A sin B sin C.
**Solutions of trigonometric equations:** general solutions of sin x = a, cos x = a and tan x = a.

questions.question: Define significant figures. How many significant figures are there in 0.00320 m?
questions.solution:
Significant figures are the meaningful digits of a measurement (all certain digits plus the first uncertain one).

0.00320 m has **3 significant figures** — the leading zeros only locate the decimal point (not significant), while 3, 2 and the trailing 0 (after decimal point) are significant.

questions.question: State the parallelogram law of vectors and find the resultant of two forces 6 N and 8 N acting at right angles to each other.
questions.solution:
**Parallelogram law:** if two vectors acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the adjacent sides of a parallelogram, the diagonal through that point represents their resultant in both magnitude and direction.

For perpendicular forces: R² = P² + Q² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 ⇒ R = **10 N**.

tan θ = Q/P = 8/6 ⇒ θ = tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ **53.13°** with the 6 N force.

questions.question: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s. Find its acceleration and the distance covered.
State Newton's second law of motion and hence define the unit of force.
questions.solution:
**Newton's second law:** the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force.

F = k·dp/dt = k·ma. Choosing k = 1 gives F = ma. **1 newton** is the force that gives an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² to a mass of 1 kg.

questions.question: Convert 5 kg into grams using dimensional analysis and state the principle involved.
questions.solution:
Same quantity in two systems: n₁[M₁] = n₂[M₂]. For mass [M], n₂ = n₁(M₁/M₂) = 5 × (1 kg / 1 g) = 5 × 1000 = **5000 g**.

Principle used: **principle of homogeneity of dimensions** — the dimensions of the quantity are the same in both systems.

questions.question: Distinguish between scalar and vector quantities with two examples each.
questions.solution:
**Scalar** — has only magnitude (no direction): mass, speed, work, temperature.

**Vector** — has both magnitude and direction and obeys the parallelogram law: displacement, velocity, force, momentum.

questions.question: A stone is thrown horizontally with a speed of 10 m s⁻¹ from the top of a tower 20 m high. Find the time of flight and the horizontal range.
questions.solution:
Vertical motion (free fall from rest): h = ½gt² ⇒ t = √(2h/g) = √(2 × 20 / 9.8) ≈ √4.08 ≈ **2.02 s**.

Horizontal range: R = u × t = 10 × 2.02 ≈ **20.2 m**.

questions.question: State and prove the work–energy theorem for a body of constant mass.
questions.solution:
**Work–energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.

W = F·s = ma·s. Using v² = u² + 2as ⇒ as = (v² − u²)/2.

W = m(v² − u²)/2 = ½mv² − ½mu² = **ΔK**. Hence W = ΔK.

questions.question: Define resolution of a vector. Resolve a force of 10 N making an angle of 30° with the horizontal into rectangular components.
questions.solution:
**Resolution** is the process of splitting a vector into two perpendicular components along chosen axes.

F_x = F cos θ = 10 cos 30° = 10 × 0.866 = **8.66 N**.

F_y = F sin θ = 10 sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = **5 N**.

questions.question: Derive v² = u² + 2as for a uniformly accelerated body.
questions.solution:
From v = u + at ⇒ t = (v − u)/a.

Substitute into s = ut + ½at²:

s = u(v − u)/a + ½a((v − u)/a)²
  = [2uv − 2u² + v² − 2uv + u²]/(2a)
  = (v² − u²)/(2a).

Therefore **v² = u² + 2as**.

questions.question: A bullet of mass 20 g strikes a wooden board at 200 m s⁻¹ and comes to rest after penetrating 4 cm. Find the average retarding force.
Find the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator working between 270 K and 300 K.
State the principle of homogeneity of dimensions and verify that s = ut + ½at² is dimensionally correct.
questions.solution:
**Principle:** every term of a correct physical equation must have identical dimensions.

[s] = [L]; [ut] = (L T⁻¹)(T) = [L]; [½at²] = (L T⁻²)(T²) = [L].

All terms have dimension of length — the equation is **dimensionally correct**.

questions.question: Define relative velocity. Two cars move in the same direction with velocities 20 m s⁻¹ and 25 m s⁻¹. Find their relative velocity.
questions.solution: Relative velocity of B with respect to A: v_BA = v_B − v_A = 25 − 20 = **5 m s⁻¹** along the direction of motion.

questions.question: A body of mass 5 kg moving at 10 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest by a constant force in 4 s. Find the force and the distance travelled.
What is latent heat of fusion? Why does the temperature of a substance not change during a phase change?
questions.solution:
**Latent heat of fusion** is the heat required to change unit mass of a solid into liquid at its melting point without a change of temperature.

During a phase change the heat supplied is used to overcome intermolecular forces (increase potential energy), not to increase the average kinetic energy — hence temperature (which measures average kinetic energy) stays constant.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of linear momentum and derive it from Newton's laws of motion.
questions.solution:
**Law:** in the absence of an external force, the total linear momentum of a system remains constant.

From Newton's second law: F = dp/dt. If F = 0 ⇒ dp/dt = 0 ⇒ p = constant.

For a collision of two bodies, internal forces (action–reaction pairs) cancel: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

questions.question: A stone is projected at 45° with speed 20 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum height and time of flight.
Define power. A pump lifts 200 kg of water through a height of 10 m in 20 s. Find the power (g = 10 m s⁻²).
State the first law of thermodynamics and write its mathematical form.
questions.solution:
**First law:** heat supplied to a system is equal to the change in its internal energy plus the external work done by the system.

Mathematically: **ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW**.

questions.question: Prove that the time of flight of a projectile is double the time taken to reach the maximum height.
questions.solution:
Time to reach maximum height: at the top v_y = 0 ⇒ 0 = u sin θ − gt ⇒ t₁ = u sin θ/g.

By symmetry, the time of descent equals the time of ascent, so the total time of flight:

T = 2t₁ = **2u sin θ/g**.

questions.question: State Newton's law of gravitation. Does it obey Newton's third law of motion?
questions.solution:
**Law:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = Gm₁m₂/r².

Yes — the force exerted by m₁ on m₂ is equal and opposite to that exerted by m₂ on m₁, so it obeys Newton's third law.

questions.question: A stone of mass 50 g is dropped from a height of 10 m. Find its kinetic energy just before reaching the ground.
questions.solution:
By conservation of energy, the kinetic energy just before hitting the ground equals the initial potential energy:

KE = mgh = 0.05 × 9.8 × 10 = **4.9 J**.

questions.question: Define the coefficient of linear expansion. A metal rod is 1 m long at 0 °C and 1.0017 m at 100 °C. Find α.
Explain the term 'moment of inertia' with its physical significance.
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia I = Σmᵢrᵢ² is the rotational analogue of mass — it measures the resistance of a body to a change in its rotational state.

Its value depends on the mass distribution about the axis and on the position/orientation of the axis. Torque τ = Iα is the rotational equivalent of F = ma.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of energy and verify it for a freely falling body.
questions.solution:
**Law:** energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another; the total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

For a body falling from height h: at the top, total E = mgh. After falling distance x, v² = 2gx so KE = ½mv² = mgx and PE = mg(h − x). Total = mgx + mg(h − x) = mgh — constant at every point.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the work done during the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas.
questions.solution:
For an ideal gas at constant temperature, P = nRT/V.

W = ∫(V₁→V₂) P dV = nRT ∫(V₁→V₂) dV/V = **nRT ln(V₂/V₁)**.

questions.question: A concave mirror of focal length 20 cm forms an image twice the size of the object. Find the object distance.
questions.solution:
For a real, magnified image m = −v/u = −2 ⇒ v = 2u.

Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u ⇒ 1/20 = 1/(2u) + 1/u = 3/(2u) ⇒ 2u = 60 ⇒ u = **30 cm**.

questions.question: What is meant by an elastic collision? Show that for two equal masses the velocities interchange after a head-on elastic collision.
questions.solution:
An **elastic collision** conserves both linear momentum and kinetic energy.

m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ and ½m₁u₁² + ½m₂u₂² = ½m₁v₁² + ½m₂v₂².

Setting m₁ = m₂ = m and u₂ = 0: from momentum v₁ + v₂ = u₁, from energy v₁² + v₂² = u₁². Solving gives v₁ = 0 and v₂ = u₁ — the two bodies **interchange velocities**.

questions.question: Define terminal velocity. What are the factors affecting it?
questions.solution:
**Terminal velocity** is the constant maximum velocity attained by a body falling through a fluid when the upward viscous drag equals its weight.

From Stokes' law v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η): it depends on the radius (r), densities of body and fluid (ρ, σ), and the viscosity of the fluid (η).

questions.question: A gas does 400 J of work while absorbing 600 J of heat. Find the change in its internal energy.
The critical angle of glass is 42°. Find the refractive index of glass.
State Newton's three laws of motion with one example each.
questions.solution:
**First law (law of inertia):** a body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force. Example: a passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes suddenly.

**Second law:** the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force, F = ma. Example: it is easier to push an empty cart than a loaded one.

**Third law:** to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Example: a rocket pushes exhaust gas downward and moves upward.

questions.question: Show that the horizontal range of a projectile is the same for complementary angles of projection. Find the ratio of ranges for 30° and 60°.
questions.solution:
R = u² sin 2θ/g.

For θ and (90° − θ): sin 2(90° − θ) = sin(180° − 2θ) = sin 2θ, hence ranges are equal.

R(30°) ∝ sin 60° and R(60°) ∝ sin 120° = sin 60°. Ratio = **1 : 1**.

questions.question: A Carnot engine operates between 500 K and 300 K. Calculate its efficiency.
Define linear magnification. A concave mirror forms a real image three times the size of the object placed 30 cm in front of it. Find the focal length.
questions.solution:
Linear magnification m = hᵢ/h₀ = −v/u.

Real image with |m| = 3 ⇒ m = −3 ⇒ −v/u = −3 ⇒ v = 3u = 3 × 30 = 90 cm.

Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/30 + 1/90 = 4/90 ⇒ f = 90/4 = **22.5 cm**.

questions.question: State the first law of thermodynamics and explain its limitations.
questions.solution:
**First law:** ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW — heat supplied to a system partly increases its internal energy and partly does external work.

**Limitations:**
- It cannot tell the *direction* of heat flow (it permits heat to flow from a cold body to a hot body spontaneously, which never happens).
- It does not define whether a process is possible at all — it says nothing about entropy.
- It cannot explain why heat cannot be converted completely into work.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the work done during the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas.
questions.solution:
For an isothermal process T is constant, so P = nRT/V.

W = ∫(V₁→V₂) P dV = nRT ∫(V₁→V₂) dV/V

W = **nRT ln(V₂/V₁)**.

Since V₂ > V₁ in expansion, W is positive (work done by the gas).

questions.question: Define entropy. Show that the entropy of the universe increases in a spontaneous process.
questions.solution:
**Entropy** is a thermodynamic property measuring the disorder of a system; change in entropy ΔS = ΔQ_rev/T (unit J K⁻¹).

For any spontaneous (irreversible) process:
ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings > 0.

For a reversible process ΔS_universe = 0. Hence entropy of the universe always **increases** in a spontaneous process — this is the second law of thermodynamics.

questions.question: A Carnot engine works between 600 K and 300 K. Find its efficiency.
What do you mean by angular momentum? State the law of conservation of angular momentum.
questions.solution:
**Angular momentum** L = r × p = Iω is the rotational analogue of linear momentum (unit kg m² s⁻¹).

**Law of conservation:** if the net external torque acting on a system is zero, its total angular momentum remains constant. Example: an ice-skater pulls her arms in — I decreases, ω increases, so L = Iω stays constant.

questions.question: A body is projected with velocity 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° to the horizontal. Find its maximum height and horizontal range.
Distinguish between heat and temperature.
questions.solution:
**Heat** is the energy in transit from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature; it is measured in joules and depends on the mass of the body.

**Temperature** measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules of a body; it is independent of the size/mass of the body and is measured in kelvin (or °C).

questions.question: State Snell's law. A ray of light travelling in water (n = 4/3) is incident on glass (n = 3/2) at an angle of incidence 60°. Find the angle of refraction.

class-11/physics/theory/dynamics.json.title: Dynamics & Newton's Laws
notes: **Newton's first law:** a body at rest stays at rest and a body in motion stays in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force. Inertia = the tendency to resist change in state of motion; mass is a measure of inertia.
**Newton's second law:** F = ma — the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force.
**Newton's third law:** for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Forces always act in pairs on different bodies.
**Impulse** = F·Δt = change in momentum. **Momentum** p = mv.
**Friction:** static, kinetic (sliding) and rolling. F_max = μN where μ is the coefficient of friction, N the normal reaction.

class-11/physics/theory/heat-temperature.title: Heat, Temperature & Thermal Expansion
notes: **Temperature** is the degree of hotness measured on Celsius, Fahrenheit or Kelvin scale. T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15.
**Heat** is the energy transferred due to temperature difference. Specific heat capacity c: Q = mcΔt. Latent heat L: Q = mL.
**Newton's law of cooling:** rate of cooling ∝ temperature excess above surroundings (small excess).
**Thermal expansion:** linear ΔL = L₀αΔT, areal ΔA = A₀βΔT, volumetric ΔV = V₀γΔT with α:β:γ = 1:2:3.

class-11/physics/theory/kinematics.json.title: Kinematics & Projectile Motion
notes: **Equations of motion** (uniform acceleration a, initial velocity u, time t): v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as.
**Relative velocity** of A with respect to B: v_AB = v_A − v_B.
**Free fall:** acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² toward the Earth's centre, independent of mass (Galileo).
**Projectile motion:** u at angle θ — T = 2u sin θ / g, H = u² sin² θ / (2g), R = u² sin 2θ / g, max range at θ = 45°. Path is a parabola.

class-11/physics/theory/physical-quantit.title: Physical Quantities, Units & Measurement
notes: **Physical quantity:** any property that can be measured — length, mass, time, force, energy. Every physical quantity has a *magnitude* and a *unit*.

**Fundamental quantities:** length (L), mass (M), time (T), temperature (Θ), electric current (A), amount of substance (mol), luminous intensity (cd). Derived quantities are expressed in terms of these (e.g. velocity = m s⁻¹, force = kg m s⁻²).

**SI base units** in NEB syllabus: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd). Prefixes: kilo (10³), centi (10⁻²), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶), nano (10⁻⁹), pico (10⁻¹²).

**Dimensions:** the powers to which fundamental quantities are raised. Homogeneity principle — every term of a physically correct equation has identical dimensions. Use: checking correctness of equations, deriving relations, converting units.

**Error analysis:** absolute error, relative error, percentage error. Accuracy = closeness to true value; precision = reproducibility of measurement. Significant figures — rules for counting and arithmetic.

class-11/physics/theory/thermodynamics.j.title: Thermodynamics
notes: **First law of thermodynamics:** ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW — heat supplied to a gas partly increases internal energy and partly does external work.
**Work in isothermal expansion:** W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁). In an isothermal process (constant T), ΔU = 0. In an adiabatic process (no heat exchange), ΔQ = 0.
**Second law / entropy:** entropy of the universe always increases in a spontaneous process; ΔS = ΔQ/T.
**Carnot engine:** efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁. Ideal efficiency depends only on the temperatures of source and sink.

class-11/physics/theory/vectors.json.title: Vectors
notes: **Scalar:** magnitude only (mass, speed, work, temperature). **Vector:** magnitude + direction (displacement, velocity, force, momentum).
**Triangle law / Parallelogram law:** resultant R of two vectors P and Q inclined at angle θ: R² = P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ, tan α = Q sin θ / (P + Q cos θ).
**Resolution:** a vector can be split into components along chosen axes: A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ.
**Scalar (dot) product:** A·B = AB cos θ = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z. Work is a dot product. Vectors perpendicular ⇒ dot product = 0.
**Vector (cross) product:** A×B = AB sin θ (direction by right-hand rule). Torque and angular momentum are cross products. Parallel vectors ⇒ cross product = 0.

class-11/physics/theory/work-energy-powe.title: Work, Energy & Power
notes: **Work** W = F·s = F s cos θ. Work done by a variable force = area under the F–s graph.
**Kinetic energy** KE = ½mv². **Work–energy theorem:** net work done = change in kinetic energy.
**Potential energy:** gravitational PE = mgh; elastic PE = ½kx². For conservative forces, total mechanical energy (KE + PE) is conserved.
**Power** P = W/t = F·v, SI unit watt (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). Energy units: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

class-11/physics/thermodynamics/concepts.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
notes: The first law of thermodynamics states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another.
For a system undergoing a change: ΔU = Q − W, where ΔU is the change in internal energy, Q is the heat supplied to the system and W is the work done by the system.
This law is essentially the law of conservation of energy applied to thermodynamic systems.
ADDED LINE: A cyclic process returns the system to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W.

class-11/physics/thermodynamics/examples.title: Worked Example: Heat Engine
notes: A Carnot engine absorbs 600 J of heat from a reservoir at 500 K and rejects heat to a sink at 300 K. Calculate the work done and the efficiency.

Work done W = η × Qh = 0.4 × 600 = 240 J.
Heat rejected Qc = Qh − W = 600 − 240 = 360 J.

class-11/physics/unit-1-physical-quantit.title: Physical Quantities — Fundamental & Derived
notes: **Physical quantity:** any property of matter or energy that can be measured and expressed in terms of a number and a unit (e.g. length = 5 m, mass = 3 kg). Measurement is the comparison of an unknown quantity with a standard (unit) of the same kind.

**Fundamental (base) quantities:** a small set of independent physical quantities that cannot be expressed in terms of other quantities. SI defines seven: length, mass, time, temperature, electric current, amount of substance, and luminous intensity.

**Derived quantities:** quantities obtained by combining fundamental quantities through multiplication, division or powers. Examples: area = length², velocity = length/time, density = mass/volume, force = mass × acceleration.

**Why a system of units is needed:** a physical law is expressed as an equation between quantities, and the numbers change with the chosen units; a standard (SI) system removes ambiguity and lets results be compared worldwide.

**SI base units (symbols):** metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature, ampere (A) for current, mole (mol) for amount of substance, candela (cd) for luminous intensity.

**Supplementary & practical units:** angle is measured in radian (rad), solid angle in steradian (sr). Everyday quantities use derived SI units — e.g. force in newton (N = kg·m/s²), energy in joule (J = kg·m²/s²), power in watt (W = J/s).

**Distinction between a quantity and its unit:** the quantity is the physical property (e.g. length) while the unit (e.g. metre) is the standard of comparison; the numerical value is the ratio of the measured quantity to the unit.

class-11/physics/unit-1-physical-quantit.title: Dimensions & Dimensional Formula
notes: **Dimension of a physical quantity** means the powers to which the fundamental quantities must be raised to express that quantity. Dimensions tell us how a quantity depends on the base units.
**Notation:** length [L], mass [M], time [T], temperature [K], amount of substance [mol], electric current [A], luminous intensity [cd].
**Dimensional formula** is written as the product of symbols with exponents, e.g.:
- Area = [L²]
- Volume = [L³]
- Velocity = [L T⁻¹]
- Acceleration = [L T⁻²]
- Force = [M L T⁻²]    (F = ma)
- Work/Energy = [M L² T⁻²]    (W = F·s)
- Pressure/Stress = [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]    (P = F/A)
- Power = [M L² T⁻³]    (P = W/t)
- Momentum = [M L T⁻¹]    (p = mv)
- Universal gravitational constant G = [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]   (from F = Gm₁m₂/ρ²)
**Dimensional equation:** an equation equating a physical quantity to its dimensional formula, e.g. [M L T⁻²] for force.
**Physical constants:** some constants are dimensionless (pure numbers or angles), e.g. π, e, refractive index; others carry dimensions, e.g. g has dimensions [L T⁻²], G has [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²].
**Important rule:** only like quantities — same dimensions — can be added, subtracted or equated (principle of homogeneity). This is the foundation of dimensional analysis.

class-11/physics/unit-1-physical-quantit.title: Uses of Dimensional Analysis & Its Limitations
notes: **Use 1 — Checking the correctness of an equation (homogeneity):** every term in a correct physical equation must have the same dimensions. Example: s = ut + ½at² → left side [L]; ut is [L T⁻¹][T] = [L]; ½at² is [L T⁻²][T²] = [L]. All terms match, so the equation is dimensionally correct.

**Use 2 — Deriving a relation between physical quantities:** relationships may be found up to a dimensionless constant. E.g. to derive how the time period T of a simple pendulum depends on length l and g, assume T = k·lᵃ·gᵇ; comparing dimensions [T] = [L]ᵃ·[L T⁻²]ᵇ forces a = ½, b = −½, giving T = k√(l/g). The constant k (= 2π) is found by experiment or theory.
**Use 3 — Conversion of units from one system to another:** using n₁u₁ = n₂u₂ with dimensional formulas. E.g. to convert a value in SI to CGS: 1 newton = 1 kg·m/s² = 1000 g × 100 cm/s² = 10⁵ dyne.
**Limitations of dimensional analysis:**
- It fails for equations containing dimensionless constants, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions — it cannot determine their values.
- It cannot distinguish quantities with the same dimensions but different physical meaning (e.g. work and torque both have [M L² T⁻²]).

- It cannot give the exact form of a relation involving sum/different of two or more quantities of different nature, and it cannot prove that an equation is truly correct — only that it is dimensionally consistent.
- It cannot determine the value of a physical constant or whether a term is additive.
**Key takeaway:** dimensional analysis is a powerful check and a guide, but physical insight (or experiment) is still required to fix constants and confirm equations.

class-11/physics/unit-1-physical-quantit.title: Precision, Accuracy & Significant Figures
notes: **Precision** is the degree of closeness of repeated measurements of the same quantity to each other — how reproducible the result is. High precision means small scatter (low random error).
**Accuracy** is how close a measured value is to the true (accepted) value. A measurement can be precise yet inaccurate (systematic error), or accurate yet imprecise.
**Difference:** accuracy is limited by systematic errors; precision is limited by random errors and the resolving power of the instrument.
**Significant figures (sig figs)** are the digits in a measurement that are reliably known plus the first uncertain digit. They convey the precision of the measurement.
**Rules for counting significant figures:**
- All non-zero digits are significant.
- Zeros between non-zero digits are significant (e.g. 204 → 3 sig figs).
- Leading zeros are NOT significant (e.g. 0.0062 → 2 sig figs).
- Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant (e.g. 2.500 → 4 sig figs).
- Trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point are ambiguous and should be avoided using scientific notation.
**Scientific notation helps:** writing 4500 m as 4.5 × 10³ m (2 sig figs) or 4.500 × 10³ m (4 sig figs) removes ambiguity.

**Rounding rules:** round off at the uncertain digit; if the discarded digit is ≥ 5, increase the retained last digit by 1, otherwise leave it unchanged. Calculations: in multiplication/division keep as many sig figs as the factor with fewest; in addition/subtraction keep the least number of decimal places.
**Example calculation:** (2.55 m × 3.0 m) = 7.65 m² → reported as 7.7 m² (2 sig figs, limited by 3.0).

class-11/physics/unit-1-physical-quantit.title: Errors in Measurement, Scientific Notation & Order of Magnitude
notes: **Error** is the difference between the measured value and the true value of a quantity. Errors are broadly classified as systematic (repeatable, due to instruments, procedural or personal — correctable) and random (unpredictable fluctuations — reduced by taking the mean).
**Absolute error:** Δa = |a_mean − a_i| for an individual observation a_i. It is the magnitude of the deviation from the mean value.
**Mean/mean absolute error:** Δa_mean = (|Δa₁| + |Δa₂| + … + |Δaₙ|)/n; the result is reported as (a_mean ± Δa_mean) in the appropriate unit.
**Relative error:** Δa_mean / a_mean — a dimensionless fraction comparing the error to the value.
**Percentage error:** (Δa_mean / a_mean) × 100%.
**Combined uncertainties (brief):** in addition/subtraction, absolute errors add; in multiplication/division/powers, the percentage errors (or relative errors) add.

**Scientific notation:** a number is written as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n (an integer) is the order of magnitude. It makes very large and very small numbers compact and states significant figures clearly.

**Order of magnitude:** the power of ten closest to the value, estimated by rounding the coefficient. E.g. radius of Earth ≈ 6.4 × 10⁶ m → order 10⁶ m. An atom's radius ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m. Order of magnitude lets one compare vastly different scales without full precision.
**Why it matters for mechanics:** writing 0.0006 kg as 6 × 10⁻⁴ kg avoids counting leading zeros as significant and makes unit conversions simpler.

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Heat (H) — Mass and Temperature Dependency
notes: **Mass Dependency:** Heat absorbed/released (H) is directly proportional to mass (m): H ∝ m
**Temperature Dependency:** H is directly proportional to the change in temperature (Δθ): H ∝ Δθ, where Δθ = θ₂ − θ₁ (final − initial)
**Combined relation:** H ∝ m·Δθ → introducing specific heat capacity (s or c) as the constant of proportionality gives **H = m·c·Δθ**

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Specific Heat Capacity (c) — Definition & Key Values
notes: **Formula:** H = m·c·Δθ
**Definition:** Setting m = 1 and Δθ = 1 gives c = H, so specific heat capacity is the heat energy required to raise the temperature of a unit mass of a substance by 1°C (or 1 K)
**Water:** c = 1 cal/g°C (CGS) = 4200 J/kg·K (SI) — unusually high, which is why water resists temperature change and is used as a coolant
**Ice:** c = 0.5 cal/g°C (CGS) = 2100 J/kg·K (SI)

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Specific Heat Capacity — Units & Dimensional Formula
notes: **CGS unit:** cal·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹
**SI unit:** J·kg⁻¹·K⁻¹ (equivalently J·kg⁻¹·°C⁻¹ since it's a temperature *difference*)
**Dimensional formula:** c = H/(m·Δθ) = [ML²T⁻²]/([M][K]) = **[M⁰L²T⁻²K⁻¹]**
Being independent of mass in the dimensional formula reflects that c is an *intensive* property — a property of the material, not the amount of it

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Heat Capacity (Thermal Capacity, C′)
notes: **Distinction:** specific heat capacity (c) is defined per unit mass; heat capacity (C′) is for the *entire* mass of a given object
**Formula:** C′ = m·c
**Heat exchanged:** H = C′·Δθ

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Principle of Calorimetry (Method of Mixtures)
notes: **Statement:** when two bodies at different temperatures are brought into thermal contact, they exchange heat until thermal equilibrium — the hotter body loses heat, the colder body gains heat
**Core condition:** if no heat escapes to the surroundings, **Heat lost by hot body = Heat gained by cold body**
**Governing law:** this follows directly from the Principle of Conservation of Energy
**Working equation:** m₁c₁(θ₁ − θₘ) = m₂c₂(θₘ − θ₂), where θₘ is the final equilibrium (mixture) temperature

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Newton's Law of Cooling — Statement
notes: **Statement:** the rate of loss of heat of a body is directly proportional to the difference between the body's temperature (θ) and the surrounding temperature (θ₀), for small differences
**Proportionality:** −dH/dt ∝ (θ − θ₀)
**With constant K:** −dH/dt = K(θ − θ₀) --- (Equation 1)
**K (proportionality constant)** depends on: (i) nature of the body — material and surface texture, and (ii) exposed surface area — a larger surface area increases the cooling rate

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Newton's Law of Cooling — Derivation of Rate of Fall of Temperature
notes: Let m = mass, c = specific heat capacity of the body
If the body loses heat −dH in a small time dt, its temperature falls by −dθ, so: −dH = mc(−dθ)
Dividing by dt: −dH/dt = −mc·(dθ/dt) --- (Equation 2)
Substituting Equation 2 into −dH/dt = K(θ − θ₀) gives: **−mc·(dθ/dt) = K(θ − θ₀)** --- (Equation 3)
The negative sign shows the temperature is falling — a downward trend over time

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Newton's Law of Cooling — Identical Cooling Conditions
notes: If two different bodies (masses m₁, m₂; specific heat capacities c₁, c₂) are cooled under identical conditions — same surface area, material texture, and temperature difference from the surroundings — their **rate of heat loss** is equal:
(m₁c₁·dθ/dt)₁ = (m₂c₂·dθ/dt)₂ --- (Equation 4)
Equal rate of heat loss does NOT mean equal rate of temperature fall — the body with the lower m·c value shows a faster dθ/dt

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Newton's Law of Cooling — Purpose & Real-World Applications
notes: This law lets you predict exactly how fast an object will cool down over time
**Forensics:** estimates a victim's time of death by measuring body temperature decay
**Engineering:** designs safe cooling systems for car engines, computers, and nuclear reactors
**Food industry:** determines how quickly cooked food or pasteurized milk must be chilled
**Everyday life:** predicts how long a cup of coffee stays warm in a cold room

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Newton's Law of Cooling — Exponential Solution & Graph
notes: Rearranging Equation 3 isolates the rate of temperature fall: dθ/dt = −(K/mc)(θ − θ₀)
Solving this separable equation shows the temperature drops **exponentially** with time: θ − θ₀ = (θ₁ − θ₀)·e^(−Kt/mc)
**Shape of the curve:** temperature falls quickly at first, then slows down as it approaches the surrounding (room) temperature — the curve gets closer and closer to θ₀ but never quite crosses it

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Finding an Unknown Specific Heat Capacity by Comparing Cooling Rates
notes: Because K and (θ − θ₀) are identical for two bodies cooled under identical conditions, m₁c₁(dθ/dt)₁ = m₂c₂(dθ/dt)₂ lets you find an unknown specific heat capacity **without measuring heat energy in Joules at all**

**Requires knowing:** the mass and specific heat of a reference liquid — usually water (m₁, c₁); the mass of the unknown liquid (m₂); and both cooling rates (dθ/dt), measured with a stopwatch and thermometer
**Rearranged formula:** c₂ = [m₁c₁(dθ/dt)₁] / [m₂(dθ/dt)₂]

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Measuring Cooling Rate in the Lab (Time-Based 'Method of Cooling')
notes: In practice, dθ/dt isn't measured directly — instead, measure the time (t) taken for the temperature to fall across a fixed, identical range for both liquids (e.g. 60°C → 50°C)
(dθ/dt)₁ = Δθ/t₁ and (dθ/dt)₂ = Δθ/t₂
Since Δθ is the same for both, substituting these into m₁c₁(dθ/dt)₁ = m₂c₂(dθ/dt)₂ cancels Δθ out, leaving the practical experimental formula: **m₁c₁/t₁ = m₂c₂/t₂**

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Limitations of Newton's Law of Cooling
notes: **Small temperature difference:** the law only holds accurately if the gap between the body and its surroundings is small — usually less than 30°C
**Constant surroundings:** the surrounding temperature (θ₀) must stay strictly constant throughout the entire cooling process
**Medium:** commonly applied to liquids, but more generally it holds for any body cooling by convection or radiation in a fluid medium, provided the cooling conditions stay uniform

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Water Equivalent (W) — Definition & Derivation
notes: **Definition:** the mass of water that would absorb or release the same amount of heat (H) as a given object, for the same temperature change (Δθ)
**For the body:** H = m·c·Δθ
**For the equivalent mass of water:** H = W·c_w·Δθ
Since H and Δθ are identical in both cases: m·c·Δθ = W·c_w·Δθ → cancelling Δθ gives **W = (m·c)/c_w**
**Note:** in the CGS system, c_w = 1 cal/g°C, so W is numerically equal to m·c

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q: Why does Newton's Law of Cooling fail for large temperature differences?
notes: The law assumes (θ − θ₀) is small — typically within about 30°C of the surroundings — and that cooling happens mainly by natural convection and radiation, not forced convection
For large differences, radiative loss actually follows the Stefan–Boltzmann law, where the rate depends on (θ⁴ − θ₀⁴), not simply (θ − θ₀), so the linear approximation breaks down

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q: Derive the exponential form of temperature fall from Newton's Law of Cooling
notes: Starting from −mc·(dθ/dt) = K(θ − θ₀), separate variables: dθ/(θ − θ₀) = −(K/mc) dt
Integrating from θ₁ at t = 0 to θ at time t: ln[(θ − θ₀)/(θ₁ − θ₀)] = −(K/mc)t
**Result:** θ − θ₀ = (θ₁ − θ₀)·e^(−Kt/mc) — temperature approaches the surrounding temperature exponentially, never crossing it

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q: In calorimetry, why isn't the equilibrium temperature just the average of the two initial temperatures?
notes: Because heat lost = heat gained depends on the m·c product of each body, not just its temperature
**General result:** θₘ = (m₁c₁θ₁ + m₂c₂θ₂)/(m₁c₁ + m₂c₂) — a weighted average, weighted by each body's heat capacity
It only reduces to a simple average of θ₁ and θ₂ in the special case where m₁c₁ = m₂c₂

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q: Equal-mass aluminium and copper spheres — which cools faster?
notes: **Setup:** aluminium (c = 900 J/kg·K) and copper (c = 390 J/kg·K) spheres of equal mass are heated to the same temperature and cooled under identical conditions
Identical conditions ⇒ same rate of heat loss (dH/dt) for both spheres at a given instant, by Newton's Law of Cooling
But −dH/dt = mc·(dθ/dt), so dθ/dt = (dH/dt)/(mc) — for the same dH/dt, a smaller c gives a larger dθ/dt
**Answer: Copper (lower c) cools faster** — its temperature falls more quickly even though it isn't losing heat energy any faster than the aluminium sphere

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q: State the assumptions behind Newton's Law of Cooling
notes: The temperature difference between the body and surroundings is small
Heat is lost mainly by convection and radiation, not conduction
The surrounding temperature remains constant throughout cooling
No phase change occurs in the body during cooling

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q (worked example): Find the specific heat capacity of a metal piece dropped into water
notes: **Setup:** a 200 g metal piece at 100°C is dropped into 500 g of water at 25°C (calorimeter heat capacity negligible). Final temperature is 30°C. (c_water = 4200 J/kg·K)
By the principle of calorimetry: Heat lost by metal = Heat gained by water
m_metal·c_metal·(100 − 30) = m_water·c_water·(30 − 25)
**Answer: c = 750 J/kg·K**

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q: Derive the working formula used in the 'method of cooling' experiment
notes: Start from the identical-conditions result: m₁c₁(dθ/dt)₁ = m₂c₂(dθ/dt)₂
Replace each cooling rate with its time-based form: (dθ/dt)₁ = Δθ/t₁ and (dθ/dt)₂ = Δθ/t₂, where Δθ is the same fixed temperature range for both liquids
Substituting and cancelling Δθ from both sides: m₁c₁/t₁ = m₂c₂/t₂
**Solving for the unknown:** c₂ = (m₁c₁·t₂)/(m₂·t₁) — only masses, water's known c₁, and the two cooling times are needed

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q: Why does temperature approach but never mathematically reach the surrounding temperature?
notes: The solution θ − θ₀ = (θ₁ − θ₀)·e^(−Kt/mc) is an exponential decay — it approaches zero asymptotically as t → ∞, but never equals exactly zero for any finite time

Physically, as θ gets very close to θ₀, the driving temperature difference (θ − θ₀) shrinks toward zero, so the rate of heat loss also shrinks toward zero — cooling effectively stalls near room temperature well before the math says it's 'finished'

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q: Why must the container shape, surface texture AND temperature range be identical in the cooling-rate experiment?
notes: K depends on the nature of the body's surface (material, texture) and its exposed surface area — mismatched containers or surfaces would give each liquid a different K
The cooling rate dθ/dt also depends on (θ − θ₀), so an unequal temperature range would make the two rates incomparable even if K matched
If either condition isn't met, the K and (θ − θ₀) terms don't cancel out correctly, and m₁c₁/t₁ = m₂c₂/t₂ would give a wrong value for the unknown specific heat

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q (worked example): Find the specific heat capacity of an unknown oil using the method of cooling
notes: **Setup:** a calorimeter with 100 g of water (c₁ = 1.0 cal/g°C) cools from 60°C to 50°C in 200 s. The same calorimeter with 80 g of an unknown oil cools over the same range in 140 s under identical conditions.
Known values: m₁ = 100 g, c₁ = 1.0 cal/g°C, t₁ = 200 s, m₂ = 80 g, t₂ = 140 s
Using m₁c₁/t₁ = m₂c₂/t₂: (100 × 1.0)/200 = (80 × c₂)/140
Simplify the water side: 0.5 = (80 × c₂)/140
**Answer: c₂ = 0.875 cal/g°C**

class-11/physics/unit-11-quantity-of-hea.title: Q: Brass vs wooden block — which cools faster, and why does this matter for 'water equivalent'?
notes: **Setup:** a brass block (100 g) and a wooden block (100 g) are both initially at 100°C and left in the same room

Wood has a much lower thermal conductivity and typically a lower specific heat capacity than brass, but under Newton's Law of Cooling the key factor is m·c: a lower m·c means a faster rate of temperature fall for the same rate of heat loss

This is exactly why 'water equivalent' is useful — instead of tracking each material's own c, every object can be converted to 'an equivalent mass of water' (W = mc/c_w), letting heat calculations for mixtures of different materials be done as if everything were water

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Scalars and Vectors
notes: To completely specify a physical quantity we may need to know its **magnitude** alone, or both its **magnitude and direction**. Based on this, physical quantities are divided into two groups.

**Scalar quantity**: a physical quantity having only magnitude, no direction. Examples: distance, speed, mass, density. Scalars obey the ordinary rules of algebra and are denoted by any ordinary letter.

**Vector quantity**: a physical quantity defined by both magnitude and direction, which must obey the law of vector addition (triangle law) / vector algebra. Examples: displacement, velocity, force, acceleration.
Vectors obey vector rules and are represented by a letter with an arrow overhead, e.g. $\vec{A}$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Addition of Vectors — Same and Opposite Directions
notes: **Case 1 — same direction**: let $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ act in the same direction. Their sum (resultant) is $\vec{R} = \vec{P} + \vec{Q}$; $\vec{R}$ is also called the resultant vector, drawn head-to-tail.
**Case 2 — opposite direction**: let $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ act in opposite directions. The resultant is $\vec{R} = \vec{P} + (-\vec{Q}) = \vec{P} - \vec{Q}$, acting along the larger vector.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Law of Triangle of Vectors — Statement and Derivation
notes: **Statement**: When two non-zero vectors are represented by two sides of a triangle taken in the same order, their resultant is represented by the third side of the triangle taken in the opposite order.

**Setup**: Let $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ act at a point, represented by sides $AB$ and $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ (i.e. $\vec{AB}=\vec{P}$, $\vec{BC}=\vec{Q}$), with resultant $\vec{AC}=\vec{R}$. Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$. Draw $CD$ perpendicular to line $AB$ extended.
In right triangle $BCD$: $CD = BC\sin\theta = Q\sin\theta$, and $BD = BC\cos\theta = Q\cos\theta$.
In right triangle $ACD$: $AC^2 = AD^2 + DC^2 = (AB+BD)^2 + DC^2$.
Expanding: $R^2 = P^2 + 2P(Q\cos\theta) + Q^2\cos^2\theta + Q^2\sin^2\theta = P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta$ (using $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$).
**Magnitude of resultant**: $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$.

**Direction**: in right triangle $ADC$, $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{DC}{AD} = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$, so $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}\right)$, where $\alpha$ is the angle the resultant makes with $\vec{P}$.

**Special cases**: (i) $\theta=0°$ → $R=P+Q$ (maximum), $\alpha=0$. (ii) $\theta=90°$ → $R=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$, $\tan\alpha=Q/P$. (iii) $\theta=180°$ → $R=P-Q$ (minimum), resultant acts along the larger vector.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Law of Parallelogram of Vectors
notes: **Statement**: If two vectors acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram drawn from that point, their resultant is represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal of the parallelogram passing through the same point.

**Derivation**: consider $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ inclined at angle $\theta$, forming adjacent sides $AB$ and $AD$ of parallelogram $ABCD$. Draw $CE$ perpendicular to $AB$ extended. In right triangle $BCE$: $CE=Q\sin\theta$, $BE=Q\cos\theta$, so $AE = AB+BE = P+Q\cos\theta$.
In right triangle $ACE$: $AC^2=AE^2+CE^2 \Rightarrow R^2=(P+Q\cos\theta)^2+(Q\sin\theta)^2 = P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta$.

**Magnitude**: $R=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$. **Direction**: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$ — identical results to the triangle law, since the diagonal of the parallelogram is exactly the third side of the triangle formed by $\vec P$ and $\vec Q$.
**Special cases**: (i) $\theta=0°$: $R=P+Q$. (ii) $\theta=90°$: $R=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$. (iii) $\theta=180°$: $R=P-Q$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Polygon Law of Vectors
notes: **Statement**: If a number of vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by the sides of a polygon taken in the same order (head-to-tail), their resultant is represented in magnitude and direction by the closing side of the polygon taken in the opposite order.

**Derivation**: applying the triangle law repeatedly to vectors $\vec{A_1},\vec{A_2},\dots,\vec{A_n}$ placed head-to-tail: $\vec{OB}=\vec{A_1}+\vec{A_2}$, then $\vec{OC}=\vec{OB}+\vec{A_3}=\vec{A_1}+\vec{A_2}+\vec{A_3}$, and so on, until the resultant is $\vec{R}=\vec{A_1}+\vec{A_2}+\vec{A_3}+\cdots+\vec{A_n}$, represented by the vector closing the polygon back to the starting point.

**Q. If two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ have equal magnitudes $P$ (i.e. $|\vec{A}|=|\vec{B}|=P$), find the magnitude and direction of their resultant.** This is the triangle/parallelogram law with $P=Q$: $R=\sqrt{P^2+P^2+2P^2\cos\theta}=\sqrt{2P^2(1+\cos\theta)}=2P\cos(\theta/2)$, and the resultant bisects the angle between them, $\alpha=\theta/2$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Resolution of a Vector
notes: **Definition**: splitting (breaking) a vector into its different constituent parts is known as resolution of a vector.
If a vector is resolved along two mutually perpendicular directions, it is called **rectangular (perpendicular) resolution**: $R_x=R\cos\theta$ and $R_y=R\sin\theta$.

**Derivation**: let $\vec{R}$ act at a point making angle $\theta$ with the x-axis. Complete parallelogram $OACB$ with $OA$ along the x-axis and $OC$ along the y-axis. By the law of triangle, $\vec{OA}+\vec{OC}=\vec{OD}$, i.e. $\vec{R_x}+\vec{R_y}=\vec{R}$, so $\vec{R}=R_x\hat{i}+R_y\hat{j}$.
In right triangle $OAB$: $\cos\theta=OA/AB \Rightarrow OA=AB\cos\theta \Rightarrow R_x=R\cos\theta$. Also $\sin\theta=OC/OB \Rightarrow R_y=R\sin\theta$.
Combining: **magnitude** $R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}$, **direction** $\tan\theta=R_y/R_x$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Resolution of Vectors — Finding Components
notes: **Fig(i): a force of 10 N acts at 30° from the y-axis.** Taking components along y and x: $F_y=F\cos30°=10\times(\sqrt3/2)=5\sqrt3\,\text{N}\approx8.66\,\text{N}$, $F_x=F\sin30°=10\times0.5=5\,\text{N}$.

**Fig(ii): a force of 10 N acts at 45° from the y-axis.** $F_x=F\cos45°=10\times(1/\sqrt2)=5\sqrt2\,\text{N}\approx7.07\,\text{N}$, $F_y=F\sin45°=5\sqrt2\,\text{N}\approx7.07\,\text{N}$ (here $\sin45°=\cos45°$, so both components come out equal).

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Types of Vectors
notes: **Like (parallel) vectors**: vectors having the same direction, regardless of magnitude.
**Unlike (anti-parallel) vectors**: vectors having opposite directions.
**Co-planar vectors**: vectors that lie in the same plane.
**Null (zero) vector**: a vector with zero magnitude, $\vec{R}=0$. Its direction is indeterminate.

**Unit vector**: a vector having unit magnitude (1) but retaining a direction; used to denote direction only. Denoted with a cap/hat overhead, e.g. $\hat{A}$. Along the x, y, z axes the standard unit vectors are $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Unit Vector — Definition and Worked Example
notes: A vector having magnitude 1 but retaining direction is a unit vector, denoted by a letter with a cap overhead ($\hat{A}$). Numerically, $\hat{A} = \dfrac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$.

**Example**: Find the unit vector of $\vec{A}=3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$. Magnitude: $|\vec{A}|=\sqrt{3^2+2^2+5^2}=\sqrt{9+4+25}=\sqrt{38}$. Unit vector: $\hat{A}=\dfrac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}=\dfrac{3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+5\hat{k}}{\sqrt{38}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{38}}\hat{i}+\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{38}}\hat{j}+\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{38}}\hat{k}$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Multiplication of Vectors — Scalar (Dot) Product
notes: **Definition**: if $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are two vectors, their scalar product (dot product) is $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=ab\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between them. The result is a scalar, e.g. $c=\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=ab\cos\theta$.
**Case 1 — perpendicular vectors**: if $\theta=90°$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=ab\cos90°=0$. This is the condition for two vectors to be perpendicular.
**Case 2 — parallel vectors**: if $\theta=0°$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=ab\cos0°=ab$. This is the condition for two vectors to be parallel.
**Case 3 — anti-parallel vectors**: if $\theta=180°$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=ab\cos180°=-ab$. This is the condition for two vectors to be anti-parallel.

**Dot products of unit vectors**: since the angle between a unit vector and itself is 0°: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}=1$. Since $\hat{i},\hat{j},\hat{k}$ are mutually perpendicular (90°): $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}=\hat{k}\cdot\hat{i}=0$.

**Component-form derivation**: for $\vec{A}=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B}=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}$, expanding $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}$ term by term and using the unit-vector dot products above gives $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Multiplication of Vectors — Vector (Cross) Product
notes: **Definition**: if $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are two vectors inclined at angle $\theta$, their vector product (cross product) is $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=AB\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, with direction given by the right-hand rule. The result is a vector: $\vec{C}=\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$.
**Case 1 — parallel vectors**: if $\theta=0°$, $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=0$. This is the condition for two vectors to be parallel.
**Case 2 — perpendicular vectors**: if $\theta=90°$, $|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB$ (maximum). This is the condition for two vectors to be perpendicular.

**Non-commutative property**: $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = -(\vec{B}\times\vec{A})$, i.e. reversing the order reverses the direction of the resultant vector (cross product does NOT commute, unlike the dot product).

**Cross products of unit vectors**: $\hat{i}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}\times\hat{k}=0$ (parallel to themselves). For the mutually perpendicular set (right-hand rule, cyclic order $i\to j\to k\to i$): $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}$, $\hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}$; and reversing order flips sign: $\hat{j}\times\hat{i}=-\hat{k}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{j}=-\hat{i}$, $\hat{i}\times\hat{k}=-\hat{j}$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/concepts.title: Cross Product — Component Form and Area of Parallelogram
notes: **Component-form formula**: for $\vec{A}=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B}=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}$, the cross product is the determinant $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\A_1&A_2&A_3\\B_1&B_2&B_3\end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(A_2B_3-A_3B_2) - \hat{j}(A_1B_3-A_3B_1) + \hat{k}(A_1B_2-A_2B_1)$.
**Area of a parallelogram** whose adjacent sides are represented by $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is Area $=|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|$.

**Worked example**: find the cross product and the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are $\vec{A}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B}=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$. $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = \hat{i}(2\cdot4-3\cdot(-3)) - \hat{j}(1\cdot4-3\cdot2) + \hat{k}(1\cdot(-3)-2\cdot2) = \hat{i}(8+9)-\hat{j}(4-6)+\hat{k}(-3-4) = 17\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-7\hat{k}$. Area $=|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=\sqrt{17^2+2^2+7^2}=\sqrt{289+4+49}=\sqrt{342}\approx18.5$ square units.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/notes/01.title: Quick Revision — Vectors
notes: - **Scalar:** magnitude only (mass, speed, work). **Vector:** magnitude + direction (velocity, force, displacement).
- **Resultant (parallelogram law):** $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$; direction $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$.
- **Triangle & polygon laws:** resultant closes the vector polygon — head-to-tail addition.
- **Resolution:** a vector $\vec{A}$ at angle $\theta$ to the x-axis has components $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$; $A = \sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2}$, $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$.
- **Unit vector:** $\hat{A} = \dfrac{\vec{A}}{A}$ (dimensionless, magnitude 1); $\vec{A} = A\hat{A}$.
- **Scalar (dot) product:** $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x+A_yB_y+A_zB_z$ (commutative, result is scalar).
- **Vector (cross) product:** $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \,\hat{n}$ (direction by right-hand rule; result is vector).
- **Component form:** $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = (A_yB_z-A_zB_y)\hat{i}+(A_zB_x-A_xB_z)\hat{j}+(A_xB_y-A_yB_x)\hat{k}$.
- **Perpendicular** iff $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=0$; **parallel** iff $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=0$.
- **Applications:** finding force components, displacement in planes, work $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}$, torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/pyqs/01-.title: NEB-Style Questions — Vectors
notes:
Q1. (Derivation) State and prove the parallelogram law of vector addition.
Ans: If two vectors $\vec{P}$, $\vec{Q}$ are represented by adjacent sides of a parallelogram, the resultant is the diagonal. From the geometry (perpendicular dropped on the extension of P): $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$ and $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$.

Q2. (Numerical) Two forces 3 N and 4 N act at a point with an angle of 90° between them. Find the resultant.
Ans: $R = \sqrt{3^2+4^2+2(3)(4)\cos90°} = \sqrt{9+16} = 5\,\text{N}$, direction $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(4/3)\approx53.1°$.

Q3. (Concept) State the conditions under which two vectors are (i) perpendicular (ii) parallel.
Ans: (i) $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=0$; (ii) $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=0$.

Q4. (Resolution) Resolve $\vec{F} = 10\,\text{N}$ at 30° above the horizontal into its components, $\cos30° = 0.866$, $\sin30° = 0.5$.
Ans: $F_x = 10\cos30° = 8.66\,\text{N}$; $F_y = 10\sin30° = 5\,\text{N}$.

Q5. (Definition) Distinguish between scalar and vector quantities with examples.
Ans: Scalar has magnitude only (mass, speed, work, temperature); vector has magnitude and direction (velocity, force, displacement, momentum).

Q6. (Dot product) Two vectors $\vec{A}=3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}$. Find the angle between them.
Ans: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=3+8=11$; $|\vec{A}|=5$, $|\vec{B}|=\sqrt{5}$; $\cos\theta = 11/(5√5) \approx 0.984$, so $\theta \approx 10.3°$.

Q7. (Cross product) Find $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}$ and $\hat{i}\times\hat{k}$.
Ans: $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$; $\hat{i}\times\hat{k} = -\hat{j}$ (right-hand rule).

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/01-.title: Parallelogram Law — Worked Examples
notes: **Q1. Two equal vectors have a resultant equal in magnitude to either vector. Find the angle between them.** Let $P=Q=x$ and $R=x$. Then $x^2=x^2+x^2+2x^2\cos\theta \Rightarrow \cos\theta=-\tfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta=120°$.

**Q2. Two equal vectors are inclined at angle $\theta$ to each other. Show that the angle $\alpha$ between the resultant and each vector is $\theta/2$.** With $P=Q$: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{Q+Q\cos\theta}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}$. Using half-angle identities $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$ and $1+\cos\theta=2\cos^2(\theta/2)$, this simplifies to $\tan\alpha=\tan(\theta/2)$, so $\alpha=\theta/2$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/02-.title: Resolution of Vectors — Worked Examples
notes: **Q1. Two forces, 10 N acting at 30° above the +x-axis and 5 N acting at 45° below the +x-axis, act at a point. Find the resultant.** $F_x = 10\cos30° + 5\cos45° = 8.66+3.54=12.20\,\text{N}$. $F_y = 10\sin30° - 5\sin45° = 5-3.54=1.46\,\text{N}$ (the second force's y-component is negative since it is below the axis). $F=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}=\sqrt{12.20^2+1.46^2}\approx12.28\,\text{N}$, at $\theta=\tan^{-1}(1.46/12.20)\approx6.8°$ above the x-axis.

**Q2. Two forces, 10 N and 5 N, each act at 30° from a common reference line, one above it and one below it. Find the resultant.** $F_x = 10\cos30°+5\cos30° = (10+5)\times(\sqrt3/2)=7.5\sqrt3\approx12.99\,\text{N}$. $F_y = 10\sin30° - 5\sin30° = 5-2.5=2.5\,\text{N}$. $F=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}=\sqrt{12.99^2+2.5^2}\approx13.23\,\text{N}$, at $\theta=\tan^{-1}(2.5/12.99)\approx10.9°$ from the reference line, on the side of the larger (10 N) force.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/03-.title: Dot Product — Worked Examples
notes: **Q1. Find $|\vec{A}|$, $|\vec{B}|$, $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}|$ and $|\vec{A}-\vec{B}|$ for $\vec{A}=5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B}=4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}$.** $|\vec{A}|=\sqrt{5^2+4^2}=\sqrt{41}$. $|\vec{B}|=\sqrt{4^2+6^2}=\sqrt{16+36}=\sqrt{52}$. $\vec{A}+\vec{B}=9\hat{i}+10\hat{j} \Rightarrow |\vec{A}+\vec{B}|=\sqrt{81+100}=\sqrt{181}$. $\vec{A}-\vec{B}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j} \Rightarrow |\vec{A}-\vec{B}|=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5$.

**Q2. Find the angle between $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$.** $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=2(2)+3(3)+4(-4)=4+9-16=-3$. $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{c}|=\sqrt{4+9+16}=\sqrt{29}$ (both vectors have the same magnitude here). $\cos\theta=\dfrac{-3}{29}\approx-0.103 \Rightarrow \theta\approx95.9°$ (obtuse, since the dot product is negative).

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/04-.title: Finding the Resultant of Two Perpendicular Vectors of Equal Magnitude
notes: **If two vectors of equal magnitude act perpendicular to each other, find the resultant.** Let $|\vec{A}|=|\vec{B}|=a$ and $\theta=90°$. Using $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}=\sqrt{a^2+a^2+2a^2\cos90°}=\sqrt{2a^2}=a\sqrt2$. Direction: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{a\sin90°}{a+a\cos90°}=\dfrac{a}{a}=1 \Rightarrow \alpha=45°$ — the resultant bisects the angle between the two equal perpendicular vectors.

**Q. If two equal vectors act perpendicular to each other and their resultant is 1.414 ($\approx\sqrt2$) units, find the magnitude of each vector.** Using $R=a\sqrt2$ from above: $a=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=1$ unit — each vector has magnitude 1 unit.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/05-.title: Two Vectors, North-of-East / South-of-East Example (Perpendicular Resultant)
notes: **If two vectors of equal magnitude 2 m act perpendicular to each other, find the resultant.** Let $|\vec{A}|=|\vec{B}|=2\,\text{m}$, $\theta=90°$: $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}=\sqrt{2^2+2^2+0}=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2\,\text{m}$.

Direction: $\tan\alpha=B/A=1 \Rightarrow \alpha=45°$, i.e. the resultant lies exactly midway between the two original vectors (e.g. if one points north-of-east and the other south-of-east, the resultant points due east).

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Motion, Frames of Reference & Branches of Mechanics
notes: **Mechanics** is the branch of physics that deals with bodies at rest (statics), in motion (kinematics) and the forces causing that motion (dynamics). It is the foundation on which the whole of physics is built.

**What mechanics answers:** *If I know an object's position, velocity and acceleration, can I predict where it will be in the future?* For everyday speeds, classical mechanics (Newtonian) gives accurate answers; near the speed of light relativity replaces it, and at atomic scales quantum mechanics takes over.
**Branches of mechanics:**
- **Statics** — bodies at rest; conditions of equilibrium (resultant force = 0, resultant torque = 0).
- **Kinematics** — describes *how* things move (position, velocity, acceleration) without asking why; the geometry of motion.
- **Dynamics** — relates *why* things move as they do: the study of forces (Newton's laws) and their effect on motion.

**Particle (point object):** a body whose size and shape are negligible compared to the distances involved (e.g. a cricket ball compared to a football field). Its whole mass is assumed concentrated at a point.

**Frame of reference:** a coordinate system (origin + axes + clock) fixed to an observer. A correct description of motion requires a stated frame — an apple 'at rest' in the train is moving at 120 km/h in the station frame.

**Distance vs displacement:** distance is the total path length travelled (scalar, ≥ 0); displacement is the change in position — the straight line from initial to final point (vector, depends only on endpoints).
**Speed vs velocity:** speed = distance/time (scalar); velocity = displacement/time (vector, includes direction). Average velocity over a round trip is zero even though average speed is not.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Instantaneous Velocity & Instantaneous Acceleration
notes: **Instantaneous velocity** is the velocity of a body at a particular instant of time: v = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt. Geometrically it is the **slope of the position–time graph** at that instant.
**Instantaneous acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity at an instant: a = lim(Δt→0) Δv/Δt = dv/dt = d²x/dt². Geometrically it is the **slope of the velocity–time graph**.
**Uniform motion:** when velocity is constant, acceleration is zero and the x–t graph is a straight line.
**Uniformly accelerated motion:** acceleration is constant; the v–t graph is a straight line whose slope equals the acceleration.

**Sign convention:** choose a positive direction once; quantities along it are positive, opposite to it are negative. A body thrown upward has positive velocity but negative acceleration (g acts downward) — so it slows, stops momentarily (v = 0 at top), then falls back.
**Slopes on graphs:**
- x–t graph slope → velocity; straightening means uniform velocity, curving means acceleration.
- v–t graph slope → acceleration; area under the graph → displacement (distance when speed is constant sign).

**From a v–t graph:** area between the curve and the time axis in intervals where v > 0 is positive displacement, where v < 0 is negative displacement; total path length needs the areas added with magnitude.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Relative Velocity
notes: **Relative velocity** of body A with respect to body B, written v_AB, is the velocity A appears to have when viewed from B's frame: v_AB = v_A − v_B (vectors measured in the same frame).
**Same direction:** if A and B move along the same line with speeds v_A and v_B, (i) chasing in the same direction → v_AB = v_A − v_B; (ii) moving towards each other → v_AB = v_A + v_B.
**Perpendicular tracks:** magnitude is found by the vector triangle, |v_AB| = √(v_A² + v_B²), directed according to the closing side of the triangle.
**Two practical results:**
- Time to meet/close a gap = (relative distance)/(relative speed).
- A person who appears to be running due north on a train moving east is actually moving northeast in the ground frame — always state the frame before quoting a velocity.

**Rain–umbrella problem:** a rain falling vertically with speed v_R appears slanted to a runner moving horizontally at v_M; the umbrella must be tilted by θ = tan⁻¹(v_M/v_R) from the vertical to cancel the horizontal component.

**River–boat (crossing) problem:** the resultant velocity of a boat steering across a flowing river is the vector sum of its velocity in still water and the river's velocity; to cross the river in a straight line perpendicular to the banks the boat must be steered inclined upstream.
**When v_AB = 0** the two bodies have the same velocity (no relative motion) — this is why two cars driving at equal speeds on a highway appear stationary to each other.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Equations of Motion (Graphical Derivation)
notes: For a body moving with **uniform acceleration a** starting with initial velocity u, the three equations of motion are:
**1. v = u + at** — from the slope of the v–t graph: acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
**2. s = ut + ½at²** — from the area under the v–t graph (rectangle ut + triangle ½·t·at).
**3. v² = u² + 2as** — eliminating t between the first two equations.
**Graphical meaning (v–t graph):**
- The graph is a straight line of slope a.
- Intercept on the velocity axis = u.
- Area under the line between t = 0 and t = t = displacement s.
**Vector convention:** u, v, a, s are signed; choose up (or the initial direction) as positive. Falling bodies are handled with u = 0, a = +g downward.
**Special cases:**
- u = 0 (start from rest): v = at; s = ½at²; v² = 2as.
- Body finally at rest (v = 0): braking problems use v² = u² − 2as to find stopping distance.
- At t = 0 the equations reduce to the initial state — always check the sign of s when the body reverses direction (e.g. up and down motion).

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Motion of a Freely Falling Body
notes: **Free fall:** the motion of a body under the influence of gravity alone, with no air resistance. All bodies — heavy or light — fall with the same acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (Galileo's principle; independent of mass).
**Acceleration due to gravity g** is directed vertically downward; conventionally taken positive downward.
**Equations for free fall from rest (taking downward as positive):**
- v = gt
- h = ½gt²
- v² = 2gh
**Thrown vertically upward with speed u (taking upward as positive, g negative):**
- Time to reach the highest point: t = u/g (since v = 0 at top).
- Maximum height: H = u²/(2g).
- Total time of flight: T = 2u/g — the return journey takes exactly as long as the ascent.
- Speed on return to the launch point = u (velocity is −u).
**Key exam points:**
- At the highest point velocity is zero but acceleration is still g (never zero).
- Time of ascent = time of descent (for equal heights, same g).
- In the first second a body dropped from rest falls 4.9 m; distances in successive seconds are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 … (odd numbers) for uniform acceleration from rest.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Projectile Motion & Its Applications
notes: **Projectile:** a body given an initial velocity and then allowed to move under gravity alone (air resistance neglected). Examples: a cricket ball, a javelin, water from a hose.
**Independent components:** resolve the initial velocity u at angle θ with the horizontal into uₓ = u cosθ (constant, because no horizontal force) and u_y = u sinθ (changes under g).
**Key results (derived from the two independent motions):**
- Horizontal velocity is constant: vₓ = u cosθ.
- Vertical motion is uniform acceleration: v_y = u sinθ − gt.
- Time of flight: T = 2u sinθ / g.
- Maximum height: H = u² sin²θ / (2g).
- Horizontal range: R = u² sin2θ / g.
**Range is maximum at θ = 45°:** R_max = u²/g (since sin2θ = 1). For every other range value there are two complementary angles θ and (90° − θ) that give the same range.
**Trajectory is a parabola:** y = x tanθ − (g x²)/(2 u² cos²θ) — a quadratic in x.
**Applications:**
- Sports (javelin/shot-put thrown at ~45°), ballistics, fire hoses, and understanding why a projectile fired horizontally and one dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same time.
- For a body projected horizontally (θ = 0) from height h: time to fall t = √(2h/g), horizontal range x = u√(2h/g).
**Common exam trap:** at the top of the trajectory the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity u cosθ is not — the projectile never stops.
