class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/concept.title: Newton's Laws of Motion (Foundations of Dynamics)
notes: **Dynamics** is the branch of mechanics that relates the *motion* of bodies to the *forces* that cause it. Newton's three laws of motion are its foundation.

**First law (Law of Inertia):** a body at rest stays at rest, and a body in uniform straight-line motion stays in that motion, unless acted on by an external force. Inertia is the natural tendency of matter to resist changes in its state of motion.

**Second law (Law of Acceleration):** the net external force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration, F_net = ma = d(p)/dt. The direction of acceleration is the same as the direction of the net force.
**Mass as a measure of inertia:** the heavier (more massive) a body, the larger the force needed to produce a given acceleration — mass quantifies the inertia of a body.
**Third law (Action–Reaction):** for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; forces always occur in pairs — F_AB = −F_BA, acting on two *different* bodies (never cancel each other).
**Why action-reaction forces do not cancel:** the pair acts on different objects, so each body experiences only one of the two forces; the 'net force equals ma' applies to forces on a single body.
**Applications of Newton's laws:**
- Rocket propulsion (reaction of ejected gases pushes the rocket forward).
- a person walking pushes the ground backward; the ground pushes the person forward.
- A boat pushed back as a person steps off it (recoil).
**Units of force:** newton (N) = kg·m/s². 1 newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/concept.title: Linear Momentum, Impulse & Conservation of Linear Momentum
notes: **Linear momentum** p of a body is the product of its mass and velocity: p = mv. It is a vector pointing in the direction of motion; SI unit kg·m/s (also written N·s).
**Newton's second law in momentum form:** the net force equals the rate of change of momentum: F_net = dp/dt. For constant mass this reduces to F = ma.
**Impulse** is the product of force and the time for which it acts: J = F·Δt = Δp (change in momentum). Impulse is a vector, unit N·s = kg·m/s.
**Impulse–momentum theorem:** the impulse delivered to a body equals the total change in its momentum: J = F̄·Δt = p_final − p_initial = mv − mu.

**Why padding/crumple zones save lives:** in a collision the change of momentum is fixed, so extending the time Δt (airbags, crumple zones, long catches) reduces the average force F = Δp/Δt — a gentler stop.

**Conservation of linear momentum:** if the net external force on a system is zero, the total linear momentum of the system is constant (p_initial = p_final). Collisions and explosions conserve momentum because the internal action–reaction forces cancel.
**Recoil of a gun:** before firing, total momentum = 0; after firing, m_gun·v_gun + m_bullet·v_bullet = 0, so the gun recoils backward with momentum equal and opposite to the bullet.
**Applications:** rocket propulsion, jet engines, firing a cannon, and explaining why a person recoils when throwing a heavy object while standing on frictionless ice.

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/concept.title: Moment, Torque & Conditions of Equilibrium
notes: **Moment of a force (torque)** about a point is the turning effect of the force: τ = F × r = magnitude F·d, where d is the perpendicular distance of the line of action from the pivot. Unit is N·m.
**Torque is a vector:** its direction is given by the right-hand rule (outward for anticlockwise, inward for clockwise about the axis).
**Conditions of equilibrium:**
- Translational (no net force): ΣF = 0 (a body at rest stays at rest; its centre of mass does not accelerate).
- Rotational (no net torque): Στ = 0 about any point.

**Moment of a couple:** two equal, opposite, parallel forces separated by distance d produce a couple with moment τ = F·d; a couple produces rotation with no net translation, and its moment is the same about every point.
**Balancing seesaw / lever problems** use Σ(clockwise moments) = Σ(anticlockwise moments) taken about the pivot, together with the weight acting at the centre of gravity.
**Centre of gravity** is the point where the total weight may be taken to act; for a uniform rod it is its midpoint — this is why a uniform plank balances about its centre.

**Practical examples:** a spanner turning a nut experiences greatest torque when the applied force is at the farthest end perpendicular to the handle; a door opens most easily when pushed at its edge, not near the hinge.

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/concept.title: Solid Friction: Laws of Friction & Their Verification
notes: **Friction** is the force that opposes relative sliding (or the tendency to slide) between two surfaces in contact. It acts parallel to the surfaces, opposing the motion or the attempted motion.

**Static friction:** the force that prevents a body at rest from starting to move. It increases with the applied force up to a maximum value f_s,max = μ_s·N, where μ_s is the coefficient of static friction and N is the normal reaction.
**Limiting (maximum) static friction** is reached just before the body starts to move; beyond this, the body slides and kinetic (sliding) friction acts.
**Kinetic friction:** the opposing force once sliding occurs: f_k = μ_k·N, with μ_k typically slightly smaller than μ_s.
**Laws of solid friction (verified experimentally):**
1. Friction is independent of the area of contact (for the same normal force).
2. Friction is directly proportional to the normal reaction: f ∝ N, giving f = μN.
3. The force of friction depends on the nature of the two surfaces (roughness), characterised by μ.
4. Kinetic friction is independent of the relative speed of sliding (over ordinary ranges).

**Verification:** a block on a horizontal plank pulled by a spring balance shows the friction reading rising to a limiting value and then dropping slightly once sliding begins — demonstrating μ_s > μ_k.
**Friction can be useful or wasteful:** it enables walking, driving (tyres grip the road) and braking, but causes wear and energy loss in machines, which is why lubricants and ball bearings are used.

**Relation between μ and angle of friction/cone:** the angle of friction θ is given by tanθ = μ; it equals the angle of repose — the steepest angle at which a body just stays at rest on an inclined plane.

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/pyqs/01.title: NEB-Style Questions — Dynamics
notes:
Q1. (Short answer) State Newton's first law and explain how mass measures inertia.
Ans: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force. Inertia is quantified by mass: for a fixed force, a = F/m, so larger m means smaller acceleration.

Q2. (Derivation) Prove the impulse–momentum theorem from Newton's second law.
Ans: F = ma = m(v − u)/t ⇒ F·t = m(v − u) = mv − mu = Δp = J.

Q3. (Numerical) A 1500-kg car moving at 20 m/s is stopped in 4 s by braking. Find the average braking force.
Ans: Δp = 1500(0 − 20) = −30000 kg·m/s; F = Δp/Δt = −30000/4 = −7500 N (magnitude 7500 N).

Q4. (Short answer) State conservation of linear momentum and give two applications.
Ans: Total momentum remains constant if no external net force. Applications: rocket propulsion and gun recoil.

Q5. (Derivation) Express the limiting friction in terms of the normal reaction and the coefficient of friction. Why is μ_s > μ_k?
Ans: f = μN; static friction must be overcome to start motion while kinetic friction sustains sliding — interlocking of surface irregularities is greater while at rest, so μ_s > μ_k.

Q6. (Numerical) A force of 50 N acts for 0.1 s on a 4 kg body at rest. Find impulse and the final velocity.
Ans: J = FΔt = 50 × 0.1 = 5 N·s; v = J/m = 5/4 = 1.25 m/s.

Q7. (Concept) Why do vehicles use brakes that increase friction on the road?
Ans: Friction between tyres and road provides the deceleration; more friction (better grip) gives the shorter stopping distance via F = ma.

class-11e/mathematics/calculus/concepts/.title: L'Hôpital's Rule — limits of indeterminate forms
notes: **Statement:** If $\lim_{x \to a} \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ is of the form $\dfrac{0}{0}$ or $\dfrac{\infty}{\infty}$, and $f$, $g$ are differentiable near $a$ with $g'(x) \neq 0$, then
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$
The rule may be applied repeatedly if the quotient of derivatives is again indeterminate — keep differentiating until a determinate limit appears.
**Example 1 — classic 0/0:** $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\sin x}{x} = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\cos x}{1} = 1$
**Example 2 — repeated use:** $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{e^x - 1 - x}{x^2} = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{e^x - 1}{2x} = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{e^x}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$
**Example 3 — ∞/∞:** $\lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{\ln x}{x} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1/x}{1} = 0$

**Caution:** L'Hôpital's rule applies ONLY to $\dfrac{0}{0}$ or $\dfrac{\infty}{\infty}$. Other forms ($0 \cdot \infty$, $\infty - \infty$, $1^\infty$, …) must first be rewritten into one of these two forms before differentiating.

notes:
**Q1. If $A = 5i + 4j$ and $B = 4i + 6j$ then find the magnitudes of (a) A, (b) B, (c) $A + B$, (d) $A - B$.**

**Answer:** (a) $\sqrt{41}$ (b) $\sqrt{52}$ (c) $\sqrt{181}$ (d) $\sqrt{5}$

**Solution:**
(a) $|A| = \sqrt{5^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{41}$.
(b) $|B| = \sqrt{4^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{52}$.
(c) $A+B = 9i + 10j$, Magnitude $= \sqrt{9^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{181}$.
(d) $A-B = i - 2j$, Magnitude $= \sqrt{1^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{5}$.

**Q2. Find the scalar product of the two vectors: $A = 4.00i + 3.00j$ and $B = 5.00i - 2.00j$. Also find the angle between them.**

**Answer:** 14, $\theta = 58.67°$

**Solution:** Scalar dot product $A \cdot B = (4.00)(5.00) + (3.00)(-2.00) = 20 - 6 = 14$. Magnitudes: $|A| = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$, $|B| = \sqrt{5^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.385$. $\cos(\theta) = 14 / (5 \cdot \sqrt{29}) = 14 / 26.925 = 0.520$. $\theta = \cos^{-1}(0.520) \approx 58.67°$.

**Q3. Find $\lambda$ if the vectors $A = 2i + j + k$ and $B = i + 4j + \lambda k$ are mutually perpendicular.**

**Answer:** $\lambda = -6$

**Solution:** Perpendicular vectors demand a dot product equal to zero. $A \cdot B = (2)(1) + (1)(4) + (1)(\lambda) = 0 \Rightarrow 2 + 4 + \lambda = 0 \Rightarrow 6 + \lambda = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = -6$.

**Q4. Find the value of $\lambda$ in the unit vector $0.4i + 0.8j + \lambda k$.**

**Answer:** $\sqrt{0.2}$

**Solution:** A unit vector maintains a net total magnitude equal to 1. Therefore: $\sqrt{0.4^2 + 0.8^2 + \lambda^2} = 1 \Rightarrow 0.16 + 0.64 + \lambda^2 = 1 \Rightarrow 0.80 + \lambda^2 = 1 \Rightarrow \lambda^2 = 0.20 \Rightarrow \lambda = \sqrt{0.2}$.

**Q5. Find the angle between the two vectors $A = 3i + 4j + 5k$ and $B = 3i + 4j - 5k$.**

**Answer:** $\theta = 90°$

**Solution:** Evaluate the dot product: $A \cdot B = (3)(3) + (4)(4) + (5)(-5) = 9 + 16 - 25 = 0$. Since the scalar dot product yields exactly zero, the vectors are completely orthogonal, meaning $\theta = 90°$.

**Q6. A force 50N acting on a body at 30° North of East. What are the Eastward and Northward components of the force?**

**Answer:** 43.3N, 25N

**Solution:** Eastward component (horizontal x-axis): $F_{east} = F \cdot \cos(30°) = 50 \cdot (\sqrt{3} / 2) \approx 43.3$N. Northward component (vertical y-axis): $F_{north} = F \cdot \sin(30°) = 50 \cdot 0.5 = 25$N.

notes:
**Q8. If three force vectors $F_1 = (2i + 4j)$ N, $F_2 = (i - 3j)$ N and $F_3 = (-12i + 5j)$ N satisfy the relation $mF_1 + nF_2 + F_3 = 0$, determine the values of m and n.**

**Answer:** $m = 31/10$, $n = 29/5$

**Solution:** Expand component equations: x-axis: $m(2) + n(1) - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow 2m + n = 12$. y-axis: $m(4) + n(-3) + 5 = 0 \Rightarrow 4m - 3n = -5$. Multiplying the first equation by 3 yields $6m + 3n = 36$. Adding that to the second equation reveals: $10m = 31 \Rightarrow m = 31/10$. Substitute back: $2(31/10) + n = 12 \Rightarrow 31/5 + n = 12 \Rightarrow n = 12 - 31/5 = 29/5$.

**Q9. In fig, the angle between the vector P and the X-axis is 25° and the angle between the vector Q and X-axis is 70°. What is the resultant of P and Q if $P = 7$ units and $Q = 8$ units.**

**Answer:** 13.86 units, $\alpha = 24.23°$

**Solution:** The real relative angular separation between P and Q is $\theta = 70° - 25° = 45°$. Using the law of cosines: $R = \sqrt{7^2 + 8^2 + 2(7)(8)\cos(45°)} = \sqrt{49 + 64 + 112 \times 0.707} = \sqrt{113 + 79.19} = \sqrt{192.19} \approx 13.86$ units. Direction relative to vector P: $\tan(\phi) = 8\sin(45°) / (7 + 8\cos(45°)) = 5.657 / (7 + 5.657) = 5.657 / 12.657 = 0.447 \Rightarrow \phi \approx 24.09°$.

**Q10. A force vector is given as $F_1 = (4i - 3j)$ N. Find the vector $F_2$ of magnitude 10N which is perpendicular to $F_1$.**

**Answer:** $F_2 = (6i + 8j)$ N or $(-6i - 8j)$ N

**Solution:** Let $F_2 = xi + yj$. Perpendicularity requires $4x - 3y = 0 \Rightarrow 4x = 3y \Rightarrow x = 0.75y$. Magnitude condition requires $x^2 + y^2 = 10^2 = 100$. Substituting yields $(0.75y)^2 + y^2 = 100 \Rightarrow 0.5625y^2 + y^2 = 100 \Rightarrow 1.5625y^2 = 100 \Rightarrow y^2 = 64 \Rightarrow y = \pm 8$. If $y = 8$, $x = 6$. If $y = -8$, $x = -6$. Thus, $F_2$ is either $(6i + 8j)$N or $(-6i - 8j)$N.

**Q11. If there are two forces $F_1 = 500$N due east and $F_2 = 600$ N due north, then subtract $F_2$ from $F_1$.**

**Answer:** 780N at 50.19° South of East

**Solution:** Vector expression: $F_1 = 500i$, $F_2 = 600j$. Subtraction $R = F_1 - F_2 = 500i - 600j$. Magnitude $= \sqrt{500^2 + (-600)^2} = \sqrt{250000 + 360000} = \sqrt{610000} \approx 781$N (textbook rounds to 780N). Direction: $\tan(\theta) = |R_y| / R_x = 600 / 500 = 1.2 \Rightarrow \theta = \tan^{-1}(1.2) \approx 50.19°$. Since $R_y$ is negative (south) and $R_x$ is positive (east), direction maps to 50.19° South of East.

**Q12. The vector F is a force of 3 newton making an angle of 60° with the displacement R of magnitude 4m as shown in the figure aside. Find (i) the value of the dot product $F \cdot R$ and (ii) the magnitude and direction of the cross product $R \times F$.**

**Answer:** (i) 6Nm, (ii) $6\sqrt{3}$ Nm, directed perpendicular to the plane containing F and R

**Solution:** (i) Dot Product $= F \cdot R \cdot \cos(\theta) = 3 \times 4 \times \cos(60°) = 12 \times 0.5 = 6$ Nm. (ii) Cross Product magnitude $= R \cdot F \cdot \sin(\theta) = 4 \times 3 \times \sin(60°) = 12 \times (\sqrt{3} / 2) = 6\sqrt{3}$ Nm. By the right-hand rule, turning from R to F tips the direction directly outwards perpendicular to the page plane.

**Q13. One of the rectangular components of a vector of 100 units is 50 units. Find the other component.**

**Answer:** $50\sqrt{3}$ units

**Solution:** Using the rectangular component relationship: $R^2 = R_x^2 + R_y^2$. Therefore, $100^2 = 50^2 + R_y^2 \Rightarrow 10000 = 2500 + R_y^2 \Rightarrow R_y^2 = 7500 \Rightarrow R_y = \sqrt{7500} = 50\sqrt{3}$ units.

**Answer:** $10\sqrt{3}$ N, 10N

**Solution:** X-component: $F_x = F \cdot \cos(30°) = 20 \cdot (\sqrt{3}/2) = 10\sqrt{3}$ N. Y-component: $F_y = F \cdot \sin(30°) = 20 \times 0.5 = 10$N.

**Answer:** 10.4 units, 17° above negative x-axis

**Q22. If the vectors $(2i + 3j)$ and $2k$ form two sides of a triangle, then area of the triangle is:**

(b) $\sqrt{13}$ unit
(c) $2\sqrt{2}$ unit
(d) $3\sqrt{2}$ unit

**Answer:** (b) $\sqrt{13}$ unit

**Explanation:** Area $= 0.5 \times |A \times B| = 0.5 \times |(2i + 3j) \times 2k| = 0.5 \times |-4j + 6i|$. Calculating cross-magnitude: $0.5 \times \sqrt{6^2 + (-4)^2} = 0.5 \times \sqrt{52} = 0.5 \times 2\sqrt{13} = \sqrt{13}$.

class-11e/physics/unit-01-vectors/pyqs/0.title: Vector Physics MCQ — Page 58 (Q28–Q32)
notes:
**Q28. Two equal forces are acting at a point with an angle of 90° between them. If the resultant force is equal to $20\sqrt{2}$ N, the magnitude of each force is:**

(a) 40N
(b) 20N
(c) 80N
(d) 30N

**Answer:** (b) 20N

**Explanation:** For two equal forces F at 90°, the resultant is given by $R = \sqrt{F^2 + F^2 + 2F^2\cos(90°)} = \sqrt{2F^2} = F\sqrt{2}$. Given $R = 20\sqrt{2}$ N, substituting gives $F\sqrt{2} = 20\sqrt{2}$, which simplifies directly to $F = 20$N.

**Q29. Two forces 3N and 2N are at an angle $\theta$ such that the resultant is R. The first force is now increased to 6N and the resultant becomes 2R. The value of $\theta$ is:**

(a) 30°
(b) 60°
(c) 90°
(d) 120°

**Answer:** (d) 120°

**Explanation:** From Case 1: $R^2 = 3^2 + 2^2 + 2(3)(2)\cos(\theta) = 13 + 12\cos(\theta)$. From Case 2: $(2R)^2 = 6^2 + 2^2 + 2(6)(2)\cos(\theta) \Rightarrow 4R^2 = 40 + 24\cos(\theta)$. Substituting $4(13 + 12\cos(\theta)) = 40 + 24\cos(\theta)$ simplifies to $52 + 48\cos(\theta) = 40 + 24\cos(\theta) \Rightarrow 24\cos(\theta) = -12 \Rightarrow \cos(\theta) = -1/2$, meaning $\theta = 120°$.

**Q30. Two forces F1 and F2 are acting on a body. One force is triple that of the other force and the resultant is equal to the greater force. Then the angle between the two forces is:**

(a) $\cos^{-1}(1/2)$
(b) $\cos^{-1}(-1/2)$
(c) $\cos^{-1}(-1/6)$
(d) $\cos^{-1}(1/4)$

**Answer:** (c) $\cos^{-1}(-1/6)$

**Explanation:** Let the forces be F and 3F, with the resultant $R = 3F$. Using the law of cosines: $(3F)^2 = F^2 + (3F)^2 + 2(F)(3F)\cos(\theta) \Rightarrow 9F^2 = F^2 + 9F^2 + 6F^2\cos(\theta)$. This reduces to $0 = F^2 + 6F^2\cos(\theta) \Rightarrow 6F^2\cos(\theta) = -F^2 \Rightarrow \cos(\theta) = -1/6$, yielding $\theta = \cos^{-1}(-1/6)$.

**Q31. Two vectors A and B have equal magnitude. If magnitude of $(A + B)$ is equal to n times the magnitude of $(A - B)$, then the angle between A and B is:**

(a) $\cos^{-1}((n-1)/(n+1))$
(b) $\cos^{-1}((n^2-1)/(n^2+1))$
(c) $\sin^{-1}((n-1)/(n+1))$
(d) $\sin^{-1}((n^2-1)/(n^2+1))$

**Answer:** (b) $\cos^{-1}((n^2-1)/(n^2+1))$

**Explanation:** Let $|A| = |B| = x$. Then $|A + B|^2 = 2x^2(1 + \cos(\theta))$ and $|A - B|^2 = 2x^2(1 - \cos(\theta))$. Given $|A + B| = n|A - B|$, squaring both sides gives: $2x^2(1 + \cos(\theta)) = n^2 \cdot 2x^2(1 - \cos(\theta)) \Rightarrow 1 + \cos(\theta) = n^2 - n^2\cos(\theta) \Rightarrow \cos(\theta)(n^2 + 1) = n^2 - 1 \Rightarrow \cos(\theta) = (n^2 - 1)/(n^2 + 1)$, which gives $\theta = \cos^{-1}((n^2 - 1)/(n^2 + 1))$.

**Q32. The maximum and minimum resultant of two forces acting at a point are 15N and 5N respectively. If each force is decreased by 2N, the resultant of new forces when acting at a point at an angle of 90° with each other is:**

(a) $\sqrt{146}$ N
(b) 11N
(c) $\sqrt{73}$ N
(d) 8N

**Answer:** (c) $\sqrt{73}$ N

**Explanation:** Maximum resultant $F_1 + F_2 = 15$, and Minimum resultant $F_1 - F_2 = 5$. Solving this linear system gives $F_1 = 10$N and $F_2 = 5$N. Reducing both by 2N yields new forces $F_1' = 8$N and $F_2' = 3$N. At 90°, the new resultant $R = \sqrt{(8)^2 + (3)^2} = \sqrt{64 + 9} = \sqrt{73}$ N.

class-11e/physics/unit-01-vectors/sets/0.title: Vector Physics Short Answers — Group B (Q1–Q2)
notes:
**Q1(a). State parallelogram law of vector addition.**

**Answer:** The Parallelogram Law of Vector Addition states that if two vectors acting simultaneously at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram drawn from that point, then their resultant is completely represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal of the parallelogram passing through that same point.

**Q1(b). Find a vector that points in the same direction as the vector $(i + j)$ and whose magnitude is 1.**

**Answer:** To find a vector pointing in the same direction with a magnitude of 1, we calculate its unit vector. Let $V = i + j$. The magnitude $|V| = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}$. The unit vector is $V / |V| = (i + j) / \sqrt{2} = (1/\sqrt{2})i + (1/\sqrt{2})j$. In decimal notation, this equals approximately $0.707i + 0.707j$.

**Q2(a). What is a null vector?**

**Answer:** A null vector (or zero vector) is defined as a vector that has zero magnitude and an arbitrary, unspecified direction. It is represented as $\vec{0}$.

**Q2(b). Give the significance of a null vector.**

**Answer:** A null vector is physically significant in maintaining mathematical consistency within vector algebra. For example, if an object is at rest, its velocity vector is a null vector. Similarly, when subtracting a vector from itself ($A - A$), or calculating the acceleration of an object moving at uniform velocity, the result must remain a vector quantity, which is uniquely satisfied by the null vector.

**Q2(c). A vector A is given as $A = 4i - 3j$. Find its unit vector.**

**Answer:**
1. Find the magnitude of A: $|A| = \sqrt{4^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 9} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.
2. Divide the vector components by the magnitude to secure the unit vector: $\hat{A} = (4i - 3j) / 5$.

class-11e/physics/unit-01-vectors/sets/0.title: Vector Physics Short Answers — Group B (Q3–Q5)
notes:
**Q3(a). What is a unit vector?**

**Answer:** A unit vector is a vector that has a magnitude of exactly 1 unit and whose primary function is to indicate direction in space. It is represented with a caret or hat symbol (e.g., $\hat{n}$).

**Q3(b). For the three vectors shown in the figure, $A + B + C = -2i$.**

(i) What is vector B?
(ii) Write B in component form.
(iii) Write B as a magnitude and a direction.

**Answer:**
(i) Vector B is the missing balance component relative to vectors A, C, and the final net horizontal result.
(ii) In component form, B is resolved to $-6i + 2j$.
(iii) For magnitude and direction: Magnitude $= \sqrt{(-6)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{36 + 4} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10} \approx 6.32$ units. Direction: The vector is in the second quadrant. The angle above the negative x-axis is calculated as $\theta = \tan^{-1}(2/6) = \tan^{-1}(1/3) \approx 18.4°$.

**Q4(a). Define a position vector.**

**Answer:** A position vector is a straight, directed line segment that specifies the instantaneous position of a particle or point in space relative to a chosen fixed reference point, usually the origin (0,0).

**Q4(b). A position vector has components $x = 34.6$ m and $y = -53.5$ m. Find the vector's length and angle with the x-axis.**

**Answer:**
1. Length (Magnitude): $R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{(34.6)^2 + (-53.5)^2} = \sqrt{1197.16 + 2862.25} = \sqrt{4059.41} \approx 63.7$ m.
2. Angle with x-axis: $\theta = \tan^{-1}(y / x) = \tan^{-1}(-53.5 / 34.6) \approx -57.1°$. Since x is positive and y is negative, this lies in the 4th quadrant, which can also be written as $360° - 57.1° = 302.9°$ (or 303°).

**Q5(a). How many components of a vector be possible? How many minimum?**

**Answer:** A vector can theoretically be resolved into an infinite number of components along different arbitrary directions. However, the minimum number of rectangular components required to uniquely define or construct a non-zero vector in a standard flat coordinate space is 2 (for a 2D plane) or 3 (for a 3D volume).

**Q5(b). What will be the angle between A and B if their dot product and magnitude of cross product are equal.**

**Answer:** Given: $A \cdot B = |A \times B|$. Using definitions: $AB\cos(\theta) = AB\sin(\theta)$. Dividing both sides by $AB\cos(\theta)$ yields: $1 = \sin(\theta) / \cos(\theta) \Rightarrow \tan(\theta) = 1$. Since $\tan(45°) = 1$, the angle $\theta$ between them is 45°.

**Q5(c). What will be the magnitude and direction of $i \times j$?**

**Answer:** By the right-hand screw rule of standard orthogonal coordinate unit vectors, the cross product of the unit x-vector (i) and unit y-vector (j) yields the positive unit z-vector (k). Therefore, the magnitude is exactly 1, and its direction is along the positive Z-axis.

class-11e/physics/unit-01-vectors/sets/0.title: Vector Physics Long Answer — Group C (Triangle Law Derivation)
notes:
**Q1(a). State triangle law of vector addition. Use this law to find out the resultant of two vectors A and B inclined at angle $\theta$.**

**Statement:** The Triangle Law of Vector Addition states that if two vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by the two sides of a triangle taken in the same order, then their resultant is completely represented in magnitude and direction by the third side of the triangle taken in the opposite order.

**Mathematical Derivation:**

Let two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ be represented by sides OP and PQ of a triangle OPQ, inclined at an angle $\theta$ to each other. Let $\vec{R}$ be their resultant represented by the side OQ in the opposite order. To find the magnitude and direction analytically, extend line OP to a point N and draw a perpendicular QN from point Q onto OP extended.

**Magnitude Proof:**

In right-angled triangle QNP:

$\sin(\theta) = QN / PQ \Rightarrow QN = PQ \cdot \sin(\theta) = B \cdot \sin(\theta)$

$\cos(\theta) = PN / PQ \Rightarrow PN = PQ \cdot \cos(\theta) = B \cdot \cos(\theta)$

Now consider the large right-angled triangle QNO:

$OQ^2 = ON^2 + QN^2$

Since $ON = OP + PN$:

$OQ^2 = (OP + PN)^2 + QN^2$

Substitute components:

$R^2 = (A + B \cdot \cos(\theta))^2 + (B \cdot \sin(\theta))^2$

Expand the algebraic binomial term:

$R^2 = A^2 + 2AB \cdot \cos(\theta) + B^2 \cdot \cos^2(\theta) + B^2 \cdot \sin^2(\theta)$

Factor out $B^2$ from the trigonometric identities:

$R^2 = A^2 + 2AB \cdot \cos(\theta) + B^2 \cdot (\cos^2(\theta) + \sin^2(\theta))$

Since $\cos^2(\theta) + \sin^2(\theta) = 1$, we secure the final magnitude formula:

$R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB \cdot \cos(\theta)}$

**Direction Proof:**

Let $\alpha$ be the angle made by the resultant vector $\vec{R}$ with the direction of vector $\vec{A}$ (along line ON).

In right-angled triangle QNO:

$\tan(\alpha) = QN / ON$

Since $ON = OP + PN$:

$\tan(\alpha) = QN / (OP + PN)$

Substitute our previously resolved scalar values:

$\tan(\alpha) = (B \cdot \sin(\theta)) / (A + B \cdot \cos(\theta))$

Therefore, the directional orientation angle $\alpha$ is given by:

$\alpha = \tan^{-1}\left( \dfrac{B \cdot \sin(\theta)}{A + B \cdot \cos(\theta)} \right)$

**Q1(c). Under what conditions the resultant of two vectors is zero?**

**Q2. Let $A = 5i + 2j$, $B = -3i - 5j$ and $E = 2A + 3B$.**

class-11e/physics/unit-01-vectors/sets/0.title: Vector Physics Conceptual Questions — Page 60
notes:
**Q1. Can a vector have zero component along a line and still have nonzero magnitude?**

**Answer:** Yes. If a vector is perpendicular to a given line, its projection or scalar component along that specific line is zero, while its absolute magnitude remains entirely unaffected and non-zero.

**Q2. Is a vector necessarily changed if it is rotated through an angle? Explain.**

**Answer:** Yes, because a vector is defined by both magnitude and direction. Rotating a vector alters its spatial direction tracking, which inherently changes the vector even if its magnitude remains identical.

**Q3. Can you add two vectors representing physical quantities having different dimensions? Can you multiply two vectors representing physical quantities having different dimensions?**

**Answer:** No to addition; Yes to multiplication. You can only add or subtract physical quantities possessing identical dimensions. However, you can multiply quantities with different dimensions to form a brand new physical entity (e.g., Force $\times$ Displacement = Work).

**Q4. If $A \times B = 0$, can you say that (a) $A = B$, (b) $A \neq B$?**

**Answer:** No to both conclusively. A cross product of zero ($A \times B = 0$) simply indicates that the vectors are parallel or anti-parallel ($\theta = 0°$ or 180°), or that at least one of them is a null vector. It does not dictate whether their unique lengths are equal or unequal.

**Q5. If $A + B = 0$, what can you say about the components of the two vectors?**

**Answer:** The individual corresponding components must be equal in magnitude but opposite in sign (e.g., $A_x = -B_x$, $A_y = -B_y$, $A_z = -B_z$) so that they cancel cleanly across every dimension.

**Q6. Under what conditions can the components of a vector be equal to the magnitude of the vector?**

**Answer:** This occurs if and only if the vector lies completely parallel to one of the principal coordinate axes, making that single component equal to the total magnitude while all other components are zero.

**Q7. Can the sum of two equal vectors be equal to either of the vectors? Explain.**

**Answer:** Yes, if the angle between the two equal vectors is exactly 120°. In a regular vector triangle configuration, this creates an equilateral setup where the resultant magnitude equals the magnitude of the constituent components.

class-11e/physics/unit-3-kinematics/exam.title: Extra solution — stopping distance at a signal
notes: **Question:** A car moving at 72 km/h sees a red signal 50 m ahead and applies brakes. It stops exactly at the signal. Find (a) the retardation and (b) the time taken to stop.
**Solution:** Convert to SI: $u = 72\ \text{km/h} = 20\ \text{m/s}$, $v = 0$, $s = 50\ \text{m}$.
(a) Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$: $0 = 20^2 + 2a(50) \Rightarrow 100a = -400 \Rightarrow a = -4\ \text{m/s}^2$ (retardation $= 4\ \text{m/s}^2$).
(b) Using $v = u + at$: $0 = 20 - 4t \Rightarrow t = 5\ \text{s}$.

class-11e/physics/unit-3-kinematics/form.title: Projectile motion — master formulas
notes: **Setup:** projectile launched from ground level with speed $u$ at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal; $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.
**Horizontal motion** (no acceleration): $x = u\cos\theta \cdot t$,  $u_x = u\cos\theta$ (constant).
**Vertical motion** (uniform acceleration $-g$): $y = u\sin\theta\cdot t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$,  $u_y = u\sin\theta - gt$.
**Time of flight:** $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$
**Maximum height:** $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$
**Horizontal range:** $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$ (maximum at $\theta = 45°$).
**Equation of trajectory:** $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ — a parabola.
**At the top:** $v_y = 0$, $v = u\cos\theta$, height $H$, reached at $t = T/2$.
